Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In its second annual "Housing Underproduction in the U.S. 2023" report, the non-profit research organization Up for Growth revealed that the nation's housing deficit grew to 3.9 million homes in 2021, an increase of nearly 3% from 2019. [2] The report, which analyzes data from 2012 to 2021, highlights a significant geographical shift in the housing shortage. [2] While previously concentrated in major coastal cities, the deficit has expanded to suburbs, small towns, and rural areas. [2] This migration was accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which spurred an 11% increase in the housing deficit in non-urban areas between 2019 and 2021. [2, 3] Specifically, housing underproduction rose by 4.5% in suburbs and a dramatic 47.8% in small towns. [1, 2] In contrast, for the first time in nearly a decade, housing availability saw a slight increase of 0.3% in America's largest urban centers, largely due to population loss as people moved to smaller communities. [1, 2] <2> On October 12, 2023, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) published a WatchBlog post titled "The Affordable Housing Crisis Grows While Efforts to Increase Supply Fall Short." [1, 2, 3] This blog post, which serves to contextualize GAO's work for the public, addresses the long-standing challenge of affordable housing shortages in the United States. [1] It highlights that high interest rates, low inventory, and an increasing number of millennials seeking family homes contribute to the issue. [1] The article summarizes findings from other formal GAO reports, such as those on making manufactured housing loans more affordable and the role of the Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) Housing Trust Fund in increasing the supply of rental units for low-income households. [1] <3> A third-quarter 2023 report from ATTOM Data Solutions revealed that home affordability has worsened across the United States. [1] Major homeownership expenses, including mortgage payments, property taxes, and insurance, rose to 35% of the average national wage, the highest proportion since 2007. [1] The report also found that median-priced single-family homes and condos were less affordable compared to their historical averages in 99% of U.S. counties with sufficient data for analysis. [1] This continues a two-year trend of homeownership becoming increasingly difficult for the average American wage earner. [1] <4> On August 24, 2023, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Secretary Marcia Fudge visited the Arrowhead Grove affordable housing community in San Bernardino, California. This visit was part of a broader two-day tour of California intended to observe the impact of affordable housing programs firsthand. During her tour, which was highlighted by the rehabilitated communities of Crestview Terrace, Olive Meadow, and Valencia Vista, collectively known as Arrowhead Grove, Secretary Fudge praised the development as a model for providing dignified and beautiful homes that create a sense of safety, wellness, and hope for residents. <5> California Governor Gavin Newsom signed multiple bills in September 2023 to accelerate housing production. Among these was AB 1307, signed on September 7, 2023, which specifies that the unamplified noise from future residents is not considered a significant environmental impact under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). [2, 8, 9] The following day, on September 8, 2023, Newsom signed SB 469. [3, 16, 19] This bill narrows the scope of a state constitutional rule (Article 34) by exempting affordable housing projects that are privately developed but financed by the state from requiring voter approval. [16] These signings were part of a broader legislative effort to address California's housing crisis. <6> On August 21, 2023, the Urban Institute published a report, "Local and State Policies to Improve Access to Affordable Housing," which was produced with support from Habitat for Humanity's Cost of Home campaign. [1] The report analyzes eight recently enacted state and local policies aimed at enhancing affordable housing access. [1] Among the strategies detailed are Raleigh, North Carolina's affordable housing bond; the 2021 expansion of the Virginia Housing Trust Fund; and the Summit County, Ohio, Affordable Housing Trust Fund. [1] The publication also examines zoning and regulatory reforms, including Austin, Texas's "Affordability Unlocked" program and Oregon's "housing choices" bill, which legalized certain multi-unit dwellings in major cities. [1, 3, 4, 5] <7> In an announcement on August 2, 2023, New York City Mayor Eric Adams reported a record-breaking year for affordable housing, with the city financing 26,682 affordable homes during Fiscal Year 2023. [3] This figure, achieved through a combination of new construction and preservation deals, marked a 22% increase over the previous fiscal year. [3] The total included 12,278 newly constructed homes, the second-highest number funded in a single year since 1976. [3] Additionally, for the first time, the total housing production figures included 2,592 apartments converted to the Project-Based Section 8 program through the city's PACT program, a move that secured significant funding for capital repairs. [4] <8> ATTOM's second-quarter 2023 U.S. Home Affordability Report revealed a significant decline in housing affordability across the United States. The report, which analyzed 574 U.S. counties, found that median-priced single-family homes and condos became less affordable compared to historical averages in 98% of those counties. Major homeownership expenses, including mortgage payments, property taxes, and insurance, rose to consume 33% of the average national wage, the highest level since 2007 and above the 28% threshold considered affordable by common lending standards. This worsening affordability was driven by a 10% quarterly increase in the national median home price, which reached a new record of $350,000. This figure surpassed the previous high of $341,750 set in the second quarter of 2022. <9> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the availability of $75 million for tribal communities through the Indian Community Development Block Grant (ICDBG) program. These grants were designated to fund a variety of projects for Native American and Alaskan Native families, including housing rehabilitation, infrastructure development, community facilities, and economic development. The deadline for submitting applications for this funding was September 5, 2023. [1] <10> A report from the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, 'The State of the Nation's Housing 2023', published in June 2023, indicated that U.S. housing markets were cooling by early 2023. The report detailed a slowdown in home price appreciation and rent growth, with rental markets experiencing rising vacancy rates. Despite this cooling, both home prices and rents remained significantly elevated compared to pre-pandemic levels, exacerbating affordability issues. The study highlighted that the cost of homeownership continued to rise due to factors like increased borrowing costs, land prices, and construction expenses, which also led to a decrease in new single-family home construction. metadata.original_text: This time series records affordable housing data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-02-18 to 2024-05-05. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In the fourth quarter of 2023, housing affordability in the United States remained stagnant and near its lowest point in over a decade, according to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Opportunity Index (HOI). [1] Just 37.7% of new and existing homes sold between October and December 2023 were affordable for families earning the U.S. median income of $96,300. [1, 2] This figure was nearly identical to the 37.4% reported in the third quarter of 2023, which was the lowest reading since the NAHB began consistently tracking this data in 2012. [1] The report, which was the final in the HOI series, noted that the national median home price fell to $375,000 from $388,000 in the prior quarter, while average mortgage rates rose to 7.44%, the highest in the index's history. [1, 2] The most affordable major metropolitan area was Lansing-East Lansing, Michigan. [1, 2] The NAHB announced it would replace the HOI with a new Cost of Housing Index (CHI) starting in the first quarter of 2024. [1, 5] <2> On January 31, 2024, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the 'Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024' (H.R. 7024) with a strong bipartisan vote of 357-70. The bill contains significant provisions aimed at increasing the supply of affordable housing. Key among these is the restoration of a 12.5% increase to state allocations for the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) for the calendar years 2023, 2024, and 2025. This measure is effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022. Additionally, the act lowers the bond-financing threshold required to obtain 4% tax credits from 50% to 30% for projects financed by bonds issued before 2026. <3> The 'Affordable Housing and Homeownership Protection Act of 2024' (S. 3673) was introduced in the U.S. Senate on January 25, 2024. A press release announcing the bill was issued the following day by Senators Tina Smith (D-MN), Jack Reed (D-RI), and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI). The legislation proposes an excise tax on large investors who purchase sixteen or more single-family homes. The tax rate would be tiered, ranging from 1% to 5% based on the number of homes an investor owns. Revenue generated from this tax is intended to be allocated to the Housing Trust Fund (65%) and the Capital Magnet Fund (35%) to support the creation and preservation of affordable housing. The bill aims to address the housing crisis by generating funds to help build and preserve affordable housing units and to make the housing market more competitive for families compared to large-scale investors. <4> Freddie Mac's Multifamily division announced it met all of its 2023 affordable housing goals as mandated by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). [5] The company's performance for the year included providing over $48.3 billion in financing and more than $883 million in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) equity investments. [5] These efforts supported a total of 423,177 affordable rental units across the United States. [5] A significant portion of the production volume, 66%, was classified as "mission-driven affordable housing," exceeding the 50% target set by the FHFA. [6] Furthermore, over 67% of the goal-eligible units financed were affordable to low-income residents (earning below 80% of area median income), and more than 20% were affordable to very low-income residents (with incomes at or below 50% of area median income), surpassing both of these specific goals. [5] <5> The Washington State Department of Commerce announced a historic investment of $312.6 million for affordable housing on January 18, 2024. [3] This funding is allocated to 73 projects across the state, with the goal of creating 3,443 multifamily rental units and assisting 470 low-income families with homeownership. Specifically, $274 million is designated for 48 multifamily housing projects, and $38.6 million will support 25 homeownership projects. [3] This initiative is a response to the significant need for more affordable housing in Washington. <6> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the availability of $40.25 million in grant funding to support housing counseling services for homebuyers, homeowners, and renters. [1] The funding, detailed in the 2023 Office of Housing Counseling Comprehensive Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), is intended to be awarded to over 150 housing counseling agencies and intermediary organizations. [1, 2] These grants will help individuals and families make informed decisions about their housing needs by supporting a variety of services, including financial management, literacy, homeownership, and affordable rental housing counseling. [1] A specific allocation of three million dollars is designated for Historically Black Colleges and Universities and other Minority Serving Institutions to help address the racial homeownership gap and assist underserved communities. [1] Applications for this funding were due by February 8, 2024. [1] <7> A CBRE report analyzing data from the second quarter of 2023 revealed that affordable housing's share of the total multifamily investment market increased to 7.7% in the first half of 2023. While overall multifamily investment has decreased from its peaks in 2021 and 2022, the quarterly average investment in affordable housing during the first half of 2023 was 50% higher than pre-pandemic averages from 2015-2019. Concurrently, the average price for an affordable housing unit rose by 133% to $135,000 as of the end of the second quarter of 2023. <8> In a December 2023 report, the Poverty and Race Research Action Council (PRRAC) detailed a growing trend among states to extend the affordability periods of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) properties beyond the 30 years required by federal law. The report, titled "Social Housing Goals in State Housing Allocation Plans — A 50-State Survey," found that over two dozen states have used their Qualified Allocation Plans (QAPs) to implement these longer minimum affordability requirements. <9> On November 27, 2023, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced $25 million in Housing Mobility-Related Services awards to seven Public Housing Agencies (PHAs). This funding, part of the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program, is designed to help families with children move to opportunity neighborhoods with high-performing schools, low crime rates, and better access to jobs and other amenities. The initiative is based on research showing that growing up in lower-poverty neighborhoods improves children's academic outcomes and long-term success. The awards aim to help PHAs address common barriers to moving, such as security deposit costs and landlord outreach. <10> On November 14, 2023, The Wells Fargo Foundation and Enterprise Community Partners announced the six winners of the 2023 Housing Affordability Breakthrough Challenge, a $20 million national competition to identify and support innovative housing solutions. Out of more than 400 proposals, the winning organizations will each receive between $2 million and $3 million in grants, in addition to technical support and peer learning opportunities to help scale their projects. The diverse winning solutions include a workforce training program that leads to homeownership, new housing finance models for rural areas like the Mississippi Delta, and advanced construction technology designed to lower the carbon footprint of multifamily buildings. The 2023 winners focus on three key areas: Housing Access and Resident Support, Housing Construction, and Housing Finance, with a priority on racial equity and environmental sustainability.

In a statement, HUD Acting Secretary Adrianne Todman emphasized the department's commitment to providing tangible resources to eliminate discriminatory housing practices. The grants will enable recipients to conduct investigations, perform testing to identify discrimination in rental and sales markets, and file fair housing complaints. [1, 2, 7] A significant change implemented with this release was a new 10% cap on the annual increase of income limits in any area, a policy referred to as the "cap-on-cap". [2, 3] This measure, first proposed in a January 10, 2024, Federal Register notice, is intended to protect low-income tenants from steep rent increases and provide stability in the housing market. [1, 2, 6] The new income limits and the associated cap became effective on April 1, 2024. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In response to Governor Gavin Newsom's May 10, 2024, revised budget proposal, California's legislative leaders released their own budget plan on May 30, 2024. The legislative proposal notably included funding for key housing initiatives that the Governor's plan had omitted. Specifically, the Legislature's version allocated $1 billion for the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention program (HHAP) and approved $500 million for the Low Income Housing Tax Credit program. Furthermore, the plan rejected other proposed cuts to crucial affordable housing programs. This legislative budget package was a critical step in the negotiation process, preceding the constitutional deadline for the Legislature to pass a budget by June 15 and the final budget agreement with the Governor. <2> In a significant move to address Hawaii's affordable housing crisis, Governor Josh Green signed several key bills into law on May 28, 2024. [4] The legislative package is designed to increase the state's housing inventory by authorizing the Hawaiʻi Housing Finance and Development Corporation (HHFDC) to issue bonds for infrastructure related to housing projects, particularly in transit-oriented development areas, as established by Senate Bill 2133. [4] Furthermore, House Bill 1760 enables the HHFDC and counties to create a bond volume cap recycling program, which allows for the use of prior years' tax-exempt private activity bond volume to support the development of affordable housing. [4] Governor Green emphasized that these measures are part of a collaborative effort to tackle the severe housing shortage and expand housing options for local residents. [4] <3> On May 10, 2024, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued PIH Notice 2024-16, detailing the implementation of the Federal Fiscal Year 2024 funding provisions for the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program. [1] The notice specifies the allocation of funds across several key areas, including setting aside $337 million for Tenant-Protection Vouchers (TPV). [1] It also establishes special administrative fees for Public Housing Agencies (PHAs) to manage housing assistance portability, particularly for those with a high volume of incoming vouchers. [1] Additionally, the notice provides one-time fees of $750 for PHAs awarded new Family Unification Program (FUP) vouchers in 2024 and encourages participation in mobility-related services through dedicated fees for PHAs that develop a housing mobility plan. [1] <4> A report titled "The Bay Area Affordable Housing Pipeline 2024," released by Enterprise Community Partners and the Bay Area Housing Finance Authority (BAHFA), identified 433 affordable housing developments in various predevelopment stages across the nine-county Bay Area. [1, 2] These projects would create 40,896 affordable homes, but require a $9.7 billion investment in public funds to proceed. [1, 2] The completion of these homes would satisfy nearly 23% of the region's Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goal, which mandates the creation of 180,000 new affordable homes by 2031. [1, 2] <5> As part of the landmark Fiscal Year 2025 state budget, New York enacted a comprehensive housing package aimed at increasing supply and affordability. A central component is the 'Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers' tax incentive, also known as 485-x, which replaces the expired 421-a program to encourage the construction of new affordable rental units. The legislative package, officially adopted on April 20, 2024, also extends the completion deadline for projects vested under the former 421-a program to 2031. Furthermore, it introduces incentives for converting commercial properties into residential use and establishes a version of 'good cause' eviction protections for tenants. The budget also addresses housing density limitations by lifting the 12 FAR (Floor Area Ratio) cap for new residential developments outside of historic districts, a measure designed to spur further construction. <6> A new Colorado state law, HB24-1007, also known as the 'Harmonizing Occupancy Measures Equitably (HOME) Act', prohibits local governments from enforcing residential occupancy limits based on familial relationships. [4, 12] Signed into law by Governor Jared Polis, the legislation is aimed at increasing housing options and affordability by allowing more unrelated individuals to live together. [3, 8] The law, which was sponsored by Representatives Manny Rutinel and Javier Mabrey, and Senators Tony Exum and Julie Gonzales, does permit occupancy limits that are based on demonstrated health and safety standards, such as fire and building codes, or those related to affordable housing programs. [4, 6] This change addresses what proponents call discriminatory limits that have, for example, restricted the number of unrelated roommates in a home regardless of its size, and is seen as a way to help alleviate the state's housing shortage. [3, 7] [3, 6, 9] <7> Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass announced the LA4LA initiative during her State of the City address on April 15, 2024. The program seeks to raise private funds from corporations, philanthropic groups, and affluent individuals to purchase hotels, apartment buildings, and other properties to be converted into housing for the city's unhoused population. The initiative aims to speed up the acquisition of housing and lower capital costs by leveraging the "humanity and generosity of the private sector." At its launch, the program had already raised over $10 million, including a $3 million grant from the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation, a $5 million loan from the California Community Foundation, and $1 million from developer Stephen Cloobeck. The initiative is designed to give the private sector clear avenues to contribute to solving the homelessness crisis. <8> On April 15, 2024, Enterprise Community Partners released the 'California Affordable Housing Pipeline 2024' report. [2] The report identified 46,605 new affordable homes in the near-construction pipeline that have not broken ground due to a lack of public funding. [2, 3] To move these projects forward, the report estimates a need for $2.6 billion in state subsidies and an additional $978 million in state tax credits. [2, 4] The analysis indicated that for every dollar of state funds invested, four dollars from private and federal funds are leveraged. [2, 3]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A blog post published on January 23, 2025, details the primary federal and state grants for affordable housing available for the year 2025. The post highlights several key U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) initiatives that provide funding to state and local governments for the development and preservation of affordable housing. Among the programs mentioned are the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) Program, the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, and the National Housing Trust Fund (NHTF). The CDBG program offers resources for a wide range of community development needs, including housing. The HOME program provides grants specifically to create affordable housing for low-income households. The NHTF allocates grants to states to produce, preserve, and rehabilitate housing for extremely low- and very low-income families. The content of the blog post is relevant for the 2025 calendar year, with various application periods and funding announcements for these programs occurring throughout the year. <2> On January 13, 2025, the National Fair Housing Alliance (NFHA) released its policy priorities for the 119th Congress and the incoming administration to address the nation's fair and affordable housing crisis. [2] The roadmap aims to ensure equitable housing opportunities and foster a stronger economy. [2] The priorities are structured into four main categories: preserving governmental checks and balances; protecting established rights, including prohibitions on housing discrimination based on race, national origin, and sex; promoting fair and affordable housing for all communities; and establishing robust civil rights protections within automated systems, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), used in the housing sector. [2] <3> In the fourth quarter of 2024, housing affordability in the U.S. worsened, continuing a three-year trend, according to a report from ATTOM. [1, 2, 4] The major expenses of owning a median-priced home required 34% of the average national wage, a figure that increased by over one percentage point from the previous quarter and the previous year, pushing it further beyond the 28% guideline preferred by lenders. [2, 3] This financial strain comes as the national median home price reached a record high of $364,750. [1, 2, 6] The report, which analyzed 566 U.S. counties, found that homeownership costs were less affordable than historical averages in 98% of them. [1, 2] Furthermore, year-over-year home price appreciation outpaced wage growth in over 75% of the counties analyzed. [6] <4> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has issued a final rule requiring a 30-day notice for eviction due to nonpayment of rent, evolving from an earlier proposal. Published in the Federal Register on December 13, 2024, the rule mandates that public housing agencies (PHAs) and owners of properties with project-based rental assistance (PBRA) provide tenants with a written 30-day notice before initiating formal judicial eviction proceedings. This rule aims to create a uniform standard, replacing varied state and local requirements, and to reduce preventable evictions by giving tenants time to cure the nonpayment. The notice must specify the amount owed, explain how to resolve the issue, and provide information on income recertification and hardship exemptions. The rule does not cover the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) or Project-Based Voucher (PBV) programs. While the rule became effective on January 13, 2025, compliance deadlines are staggered to allow PHAs and property owners time to update leases. <5> A Yardi Matrix report on affordable housing, analyzing data through September 2024, found that both revenues and expenses grew year-over-year. [3] Specifically, for the average affordable unit, expenses increased by 6.4%, while income rose by 7.2%. [3] This dynamic resulted in a significant 8.1% spike in net operating income compared to the previous year. [3] The primary drivers behind the growth in expenses were identified as rising costs for property insurance and marketing. [3] Regarding rental rates for 2024, the Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) formula, which considered a nearly 14.8% change, would have permitted a rent increase up to that amount; however, HUD implemented a new absolute cap, settling the maximum allowable rent increase at 10%. [4] <6> In the November 5, 2024, general election, voters in Arlington County, Virginia, approved a series of five local bond referenda totaling $273 million. While none of the bonds were exclusively for affordable housing, the package included a $76.15 million bond for county infrastructure projects and a $72.4 million bond for transportation, which encompasses funding for the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority's (WMATA) Capital Improvement Program and local street and sidewalk improvements. Another bond allocated $83.99 million for Arlington Public Schools projects. Kansas City, Missouri, passed a $50 million housing bond that was approved by voters during the November 8, 2022, midterm elections. Other cities, including in Colorado and California, also approved housing-related funding in the 2022 election cycle. <7> An article published on October 4, 2024, highlighted several new affordable housing developments. A unique project at 203 Newport Street in Brooklyn's Brownsville neighborhood was noted as a first-of-its-kind model for New York City, combining 174 affordable and supportive housing units with light manufacturing workshops. Another featured development was the Betances Family Apartments in the Mott Haven neighborhood of the Bronx, which adds 101 affordable units. In Portland, Oregon, the 200-unit Slabtown Square community was also mentioned, with 40 of its units designated as affordable for households earning up to 80% of the area's median income. <8> On September 19, 2024, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed a significant bipartisan legislative package aimed at addressing the state's housing and homelessness crisis. While some reports cited a package of 32 bills, other authoritative sources state that over 60 housing-related bills were signed into law. These laws, most of which took effect on January 1, 2025, are designed to accelerate housing production, strengthen the enforcement of state housing laws, and address homelessness. Key provisions include streamlining development processes, holding local governments accountable with stricter timelines and penalties for non-compliance, and promoting the construction of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs). <9> The National Equity Fund (NEF), a Chicago-based nonprofit specializing in affordable real estate investment, announced it has raised over $1 billion through its Homestead Equity Fund (HEF) program since acquiring it in 2010. The announcement on September 17, 2024, highlighted the cumulative success of ten funds within the HEF program. The most recent fund, Homestead Equity Fund XIX, closed in the summer of 2024, raising $222 million on its own. This series of funds has supported the creation and preservation of nearly 8,000 affordable housing units across 150 developments in 14 western states. This achievement is part of a record-breaking year for NEF, which announced separately on January 14, 2025, that it had raised and deployed a total of $2.7 billion in affordable housing investments during 2024, creating or preserving over 16,000 homes nationwide.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> An article by Jennifer Murillo and Monica Szydlik of Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc., published in The Western Planner on March 28, 2025, details how updating zoning regulations can increase housing accessibility and production. The article focuses on refining municipal codes to address the housing shortage in the Western United States and beyond. It provides successful examples of zoning reforms from California, Arizona, and Ohio. The approaches discussed are aligned with the American Planning Association’s "Equity in Zoning Policy Guide" and "Housing Supply Accelerator Playbook". One specific example mentioned is the adoption of new standards by a City Council in December 2024. <2> ATTOM released its Q1 2025 U.S. Home Affordability Report on March 27, 2025, revealing that housing affordability continues to be a major financial challenge for average workers. [1] The report found that in 97% of U.S. counties with sufficient data, median-priced single-family homes and condos remained less affordable compared to historical averages. [1, 3, 4] This extends a three-year pattern of home prices outpacing wage growth. [1] Major ownership expenses on a median-priced home, which dipped slightly to $351,000, consumed 32% of the average national wage. [1, 2, 4] This figure remains above the 28% lending guideline commonly preferred by lenders. [1] To afford the median-priced home in Q1 2025, a buyer would need an annual income of $86,611, which is 15.9% higher than the average national wage of $74,698. [1, 2] <3> Archway Communities announced its affordable housing priorities for the 2025 Colorado legislative session in a blog post on March 18, 2025. [2] The organization stated its policy recommendations are based on its experience in financing, developing, and supporting residents in affordable housing. [2] Their advocacy focuses on three main principles, including the building and preservation of affordable housing. [2] Working with other affordable housing developers, Archway's priorities include preserving and expanding grant funds like the Housing Development Grant Fund (HDG) and collaborating on a potential new $100 million, 0% interest loan fund to support affordable housing development. [2] <4> The National Low Income Housing Coalition (NLIHC) released its annual report, "The Gap: A Shortage of Affordable Homes," on March 13, 2025. [1] The report reveals a national shortage of 7.1 million affordable and available rental homes for extremely low-income renters. [1, 4] This equates to only 35 affordable and available homes for every 100 extremely low-income renter households. [1, 2] Consequently, 75% of these renters are severely cost-burdened, spending more than half of their income on rent. [1, 4] The housing shortage affects every state, with Nevada, Oregon, California, Arizona, and Texas identified as having the most severe deficits. [1, 6] The NLIHC report concludes that the private market is unable to meet the needs of the lowest-income renters and calls for increased federal investment in housing programs. [1, 6] <5> A Yardi Matrix report from March 2025 indicates that 850,000 private Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) units are projected to reach the end of their affordability restriction periods between 2025 and 2038. This total comprises approximately 520,000 units finishing their initial 15-year compliance period and another 330,000 units concluding their 30-year extended-use period. The report, which analyzed data as of January 2025, highlights that the loss of affordability restrictions on these properties could intensify the national housing shortage. In 2025, 29,000 units would end compliance and 15,000 would end their extended-use period. Over the broader 2025-2027 timeframe, 44,600 private LIHTC units will meet the expiration of their extended-use periods in those three years. <6> A Moody's Analytics report for Q4 2024 indicated initial improvements in the multifamily housing market, with median income growth surpassing rent growth. The national rent-to-income (RTI) ratio fell to 27.4%, marking the fifth consecutive quarterly decline and a return to pre-pandemic levels. [5] However, significant affordability issues persist, particularly for first-time homebuyers. New York was the most rent-burdened metro with an RTI of 58.5%, and Los Angeles was also notably high at 33.0%. [5] <7> The "Choice in Affordable Housing Act of 2025" (S.890) was introduced in the U.S. Senate for the 119th Congress (2025-2026) on March 6, 2025. [1, 2, 3] The bipartisan bill aims to increase landlord participation in the Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) program, also known as Section 8, by offering incentives and streamlining processes. [1, 6, 7] Key provisions include creating a $500 million fund for landlord signing bonuses and security deposit assistance, and reducing duplicative inspection requirements for properties already approved under other federal housing programs. [6, 7] The bill was introduced by Senator Chris Coons and cosponsored by Senators Tina Smith, Raphael Warnock, Jerry Moran, John Curtis, and Martin Heinrich, before being referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. [2, 5] A companion bill, H.R. 1981, was introduced in the House of Representatives. [6, 7] The stated goal is to expand housing options for low-income families and improve their access to high-opportunity neighborhoods. [7] <8> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) put into effect an interim final rule that revises the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH) requirement, returning to the pre-1994 understanding of the statutory certification. [1, 3, 7] The rule, which became effective on April 2, 2025, aims to simplify compliance and reduce administrative burdens for jurisdictions and housing authorities by eliminating specific planning mechanisms like the Analysis of Impediments (AI) and other detailed reporting requirements. [1, 3] Instead, a grantee's certification that it took any action rationally related to promoting fair housing will be deemed sufficient. [3, 7] News of the rule was first announced in late February 2025, with a pre-publication copy appearing on February 28, 2025, followed by official publication in the Federal Register on March 3, 2025. [3, 1, 7] This action followed the withdrawal of a more comprehensive proposed AFFH rule on January 16, 2025. [9, 10]

United States*. Hailed as a landmark piece of housing legislation, the act aims to address the nationwide housing crisis by boosting housing supply, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding access to affordable homeownership. Key provisions include creating grant programs to incentivize local governments to increase housing supply by streamlining permitting and modernizing zoning codes, authorizing the Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program, and modernizing the HOME Investment Partnerships Program. The comprehensive bill, which bundles approximately 40 previous proposals, seeks to modernize financing systems, improve access to manufactured and rural housing, and enhance oversight of federal housing programs. The legislation will next be considered by the House of Representatives. <3> A coalition, including New York City Council Members, labor unions, and advocates, held a press conference on October 7, 2025, to warn voters about what they termed the 'misleading language' of Mayor Eric Adams' Ballot Proposals 2, 3, and 4. Led by City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams, the group argued that the proposals, while ostensibly aimed at increasing housing, would actually strip communities and their elected Council Members of the power to negotiate for more affordable housing, good union jobs, and essential neighborhood investments like parks and schools. The coalition, which included representatives from 32BJ SEIU, the District Council of Carpenters, and the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council, contended that the proposals would shift decision-making power on development projects from the democratically elected City Council to unelected mayoral appointees, thereby reducing public accountability and giving developers more influence. The full development, expected to be completed by 2029, involves renovating 54 of the original 142 units and constructing 146 new single-family homes and townhomes. It revealed that about a third of the top 30 U.S. metros are highly competitive. Key factors affecting this competition include the absolute cost of market rents, the volume of new housing supply, and the age of the housing stock. Metros with average rents below $1,500, such as Las Vegas and Houston, showed high competitiveness, while cities with rents exceeding $2,500, like New York and San Francisco, had very little competition. <7> In Rochester, New York, housing prices have experienced a significant surge, as reported in an article about a new city pilot program aimed at rehabilitating derelict properties for low-income buyers. According to data from the Greater Rochester Association of Realtors, the median sale price for a single-family house in the city reached $197,500 in July 2025. This is nearly double the median price of $106,500 recorded in March 2022. The trend of rising housing costs is also reflected in the rental market, with the average fair market rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the Rochester metropolitan area increasing by 48% since 2020 to $1,149. <8> The White Plains Common Council unanimously voted to approve revisions to the city's affordable housing program, with the news being reported on August 7, 2025. The new rules, which take effect on September 15, 2025, aim to increase the number of affordable units in the city. Key changes include adjusting the income eligibility for affordable units from the previous 50-80% of the Westchester Area Median Income (AMI) to a new range of 40-60% of the AMI. The revised program also establishes an eligibility preference for White Plains residents and employees of the city, its housing authority, urban renewal agency, and the school district. Furthermore, the policy on developers opting out of providing affordable units was updated; the cap on the number of units a developer can pay a fee-in-lieu for was increased from 25 to 35. The fee itself was raised from 125% to 130% of the Westchester County HUD AMI for a four-person household. <9> The city of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, announced it is launching an $8 million Affordable Housing Development Fund to support developers in increasing the city's housing options. [2] The initiative is financed through the federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). [2] The fund is available to qualified developers for projects involving new construction, or the expansion or enhancement of existing affordable housing units within the city. [2] While the city council had approved designating the $8 million in ARPA funds for affordable housing in July 2023, the formal announcement of the development fund and application process was made on August 7, 2025. [2, 3, 5] Applications for developers are scheduled to open following a press conference on August 11, 2025. The update, released on August 6, 2025, highlighted that nearly 80% of the law's provisions have been implemented, with full implementation anticipated by the end of 2025. This progress is part of a broader strategy that includes converting vacant state-owned land and commercial properties into housing, increasing housing development tax credits, and leveraging the MBTA Communities Law to address the state's housing costs.
